references.label: Neural Discrete Representation Learning (VQ-VAE) · selected passage

definition.title: VQ-VAE forward pass: snapping the encoder output to a codebook vector
definition.summary: The encoder's continuous output is replaced by the nearest of K learned embedding vectors, and that vector, not the raw output, is what the decoder receives.

nodes.label: ze(x)
nodes.detail: The encoder output: a vector of D real numbers. It lives in the same D-dimensional space as the embedding vectors, which is what makes a distance comparison possible.

nodes.label: Embedding space e
nodes.sub: K vectors, each of size D
nodes.detail: A learned table e with K rows, one embedding vector per row. It is shared: every latent is looked up in the same table. Its entries are model parameters alongside the encoder and decoder weights.

nodes.label: Nearest-neighbour look-up
nodes.detail: Finds the index k whose embedding has the smallest Euclidean distance to ze(x). That index is the discrete latent variable z (equation 1 in the paper).

nodes.label: Embedding ek
nodes.detail: The row of the table selected by the index k. The paper calls it zq(x), the quantised version of ze(x) (equation 2).

beats.caption: The encoder turns the input x into a continuous vector ze(x), exactly as in an ordinary autoencoder.
beats.explanation: Up to this point nothing is discrete. ze(x) is a vector of real numbers produced by the encoder network.

beats.caption: ze(x) is compared with a shared table of K embedding vectors; the index k of the nearest one is the discrete latent z.
beats.explanation: The embedding space e holds K vectors, each of dimension D. The nearest-neighbour look-up picks the one closest to ze(x), and its index is the discrete code.

beats.caption: The decoder receives the chosen embedding ek, not ze(x) itself, and reconstructs the input from it.
beats.explanation: The paper writes this decoder input as zq(x) = ek. Whatever detail of ze(x) is not captured by the chosen embedding is discarded at this step.

beats.caption: Picture a toy embedding space with D = 2 and K = 4: four embedding vectors and one encoder output ze(x) share the same space.
beats.explanation: This is a simplified model with invented coordinates. Real models use many more embeddings and more dimensions, but the geometry is the same.

beats.caption: Measure the Euclidean distance from ze(x) to every embedding; in this example e2 is the closest at 1.8.
beats.explanation: This is the comparison inside the nearest-neighbour look-up: one distance per embedding, K distances in total. The values shown are invented for the example.

beats.caption: ze(x) is replaced by e2, so the discrete latent is z = 2 and the decoder input zq(x) is exactly e2.
beats.explanation: Any encoder output that lands closer to e2 than to the other embeddings yields the same code. The continuous space is thereby carved into K regions, one per embedding.

beats.caption: The same example as a table: every one of the K = 4 embeddings gets a distance to ze(x).
beats.explanation: Each column is one slot of the embedding table. The distances are the ones drawn in the previous figure.

beats.caption: Equation 1 makes the posterior one-hot: probability 1 at the index with the smallest distance, 0 everywhere else.
beats.explanation: In the paper, q(z = k | x) is 1 for the k that minimises the distance between ze(x) and ej, and 0 otherwise. The choice is deterministic, with no sampling involved; the numbers here continue the invented example.

beats.caption: Equation 2 reads out that one row of the table, so the non-linearity maps any ze(x) to one of only K possible vectors.
beats.explanation: This is what the passage means by a regular autoencoder with a particular non-linearity: a layer between encoder and decoder whose output is always one of K fixed vectors. Unlike ReLU-style non-linearities, it is a hard selection.

takeaways: The VQ-VAE forward pass is an autoencoder with one extra step: replace the encoder output with the nearest of K learned embedding vectors.
The discrete latent z is only the index of that vector; the decoder sees the vector ek itself.
Because the selection is an argmin it has no real gradient, which the paper handles separately with a straight-through estimator.
